questions.question: What makes a good quotation for analysis?

points.text: Good quotations are: rich in language techniques (metaphor, imagery), significant to character/theme, concise (short enough to analyse word by word), and flexible (can be used for multiple points).

questions.question: What's the difference between dropping and embedding a quotation?

points.text: Dropping: quotation stands alone as separate sentence. Embedding: quotation is part of your sentence structure. Embedded quotations flow naturally and show stronger integration.

questions.question: How many quotations should you memorise per text?

points.text: Recommended 5-8 key quotations per text. Choose quotations that work for multiple themes/characters. Quality over quantity - better to know a few well than many poorly.

questions.question: After analysing language, what should you link to?

points.text: After analysing language, link to: themes (what idea is explored), character development, and context (when/why written, audience response).

markScheme.exemplarAnswer: Shakespeare presents Macbeth's conscience as a powerful but ultimately insufficient restraint against ambition. In his soliloquy, Macbeth acknowledges he has "no spur to prick the sides of my intent, but only vaulting ambition, which o'erleaps itself." The equestrian metaphor is devastatingly precise: "spur" implies motivation, yet Macbeth concedes he has "no spur" — his only driver is "vaulting ambition," where the adjective "vaulting" suggests something that leaps beyond its natural limits. The verb "o'erleaps" conveys reckless overextension, while the reflexive "itself" reveals that ambition's destructive energy will ultimately turn inward. Shakespeare reinforces Macbeth's moral awareness through his recognition that Duncan's "virtues will plead like angels," where the simile elevates the king's goodness to a divine standard against which Macbeth's "bloody instructions" are measured. The juxtaposition of "virtues" and "bloody" underscores the moral chasm Macbeth must cross. For a Jacobean audience versed in the Great Chain of Being, Macbeth's awareness of this moral order makes his subsequent choice all the more damnable — he is not ignorant of right and wrong but chooses to silence his conscience. Mark scheme: AO1 (10/10) — sustained, confident interpretation with an informed personal response; AO2 (10/10) — detailed analysis of language with precise word-level zoom; AO3 (5/5) — integrated Jacobean context linked to the Great Chain of Being.
